About Me I’m a computer scientist working on AI privacy. Lately I’ve been moving into responsible AI more broadly, because the interesting problems sit where technical work meets real societal questions. I’ve spent my career connecting people across academia and industry, and I like projects that need both solid theory and a real understanding of the domain.
What I Share on This Page My work on trustworthy and private AI systems Opinions on AI policy, privacy, and responsible AI methods Open-source tools and research artifacts Reach Out to Me! I’m open to collaborations on AI security, privacy, and responsible AI. Feel free to contact me about research, teaching, or open-source projects.

content:
Agentic AI systems can make decisions, carry out tasks, and interact with their environment autonomously. This autonomy introduces security risks that go beyond classic AI vulnerabilities, including manipulation of API interactions, misuse of external tools and APIs, unsafe data or faulty API responses, and risks from insufficient API authentication and authorisation.
This thesis reviews the existing literature on AI security and API interactions, develops a classification of vulnerabilities specific to agentic AI, and evaluates it against examples such as open-source agents like AutoGPT or LangChain.
Type of work: Bachelor thesis, Master thesis or project Field: AI Engineering, with links to Data Analysis and Statistics, Information Security, Machine Learning, and Trustworthy AI Institute: Centre for Artificial Intelligence (CAI), Institute of Data Science (IDS), ZHAW Prerequisites: basic machine learning knowledge, ability to review and critically assess literature, basic programming skills (e.g. Python) for the experiments. Experience with frameworks such as LangChain or AutoGPT is a plus, not a requirement. Language: German or English Get in touch if you’d like to discuss this topic before applying.
summary: Mapping the security risks that arise when agentic AI systems act autonomously through external tools and APIs, beyond classic AI vulnerabilities.
title: AI Security: Risks of Agentic AI Systems Interacting with External Tools and APIs

content:
Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) enable direct communication between the brain and external devices, and are used in medical, assistive, and neurofeedback applications. Because brain data is highly sensitive, this project explores federated learning, a decentralised approach that trains models on local devices without sharing raw data, as a way to improve BCI privacy. Data and code from previous BCI experiments are already available to build on.
Tasks include a literature review of federated learning and privacy in BCI systems, setting up the development environment, implementing a federated learning framework tailored to BCI applications, running experiments comparing accuracy, efficiency, and privacy preservation against traditional centralised approaches, and writing up the results. With good results, the outcome could be used as a demonstrator at public events, a basis for future projects, or a joint publication with the supervisors.
Type of work: Bachelor thesis, Master thesis or project Field: Machine Learning, with links to AI Engineering, Medical Technology, and Trustworthy AI Institute: Centre for Artificial Intelligence (CAI), Institute of Data Science (IDS), ZHAW Prerequisites: good Python programming skills; no prior machine learning/AI knowledge required. Curiosity for research work, a pragmatic approach to experimentation, and a strong track record in your study programme are expected. Language: English Get in touch if you’d like to discuss this topic before applying.
summary: Applying federated learning to protect the privacy of brain-computer interface (BCI) data, with data and code from previous BCI experiments already available.
title: Enhancing Privacy in Brain-Computer Interfaces Using Federated Learning

content:
This project investigates how bias propagates in multi-agent LLM systems when agents interact through external tools such as APIs, databases, or retrieval models. Using open-source agent frameworks, experiments will measure whether biased tools influence the agents that use them, whether de-biasing the tools alone is sufficient, and whether differently-initialised agents converge toward a dominant bias over time.
Type of work: Bachelor thesis, Master thesis or project Field: Trustworthy AI, with links to AI Engineering and Machine Learning Institute: Institute of Data Science (IDS), Centre for Artificial Intelligence (CAI), ZHAW Prerequisites: basic machine learning knowledge, ability to review and critically assess literature, basic programming skills (e.g. Python) for the experiments. Experience with frameworks such as LangChain or AutoGPT is a plus, not a requirement. Language: German or English Get in touch if you’d like to discuss this topic before applying.
summary: How bias spreads through multi-agent LLM systems when agents rely on external tools such as APIs, databases, or retrieval models.
title: Fairness Bias in Agentic AI Systems

content:
For most of its history, machine learning produced models that sat still and waited to be asked questions. You sent data in; a prediction came out. The model had no memory of past interactions, no ability to take actions in the world, and no access to anything beyond what you explicitly provided.
That is no longer the typical case. The systems I spend a lot of my time thinking about at SCRAI are agentic: they can use tools, maintain state across interactions, delegate subtasks to other agents, and take actions — browsing, writing, executing code, sending messages — with real-world consequences. The capabilities are genuinely impressive, and they create a genuinely new privacy landscape.
I want to be precise about what I mean by “new.” The privacy concerns of static ML models — training data memorisation, membership inference, model inversion — have not gone away. Agentic systems add to them; they do not replace them. But the addition is significant.
The data minimisation problem One of the foundational principles of data protection law — enshrined in GDPR Article 5 — is data minimisation: collect only what you need, for as long as you need it, for the purposes you specified.
This principle was designed for systems where a human engineer explicitly decides what data to collect and why. It maps poorly onto agentic systems, which acquire and process information incidentally, as a byproduct of completing tasks. An agent helping you plan a trip learns your travel preferences, your budget, your schedule, your dietary restrictions, and — if it books accommodation — your home address. It did not ask for this information; it accumulated it in the course of being useful.
The agent’s memory system then becomes a concentrated, structured record of things you never deliberately chose to share. This is different in kind from, say, a search engine that logs your queries. The agent synthesises, infers, and acts on information in ways that can reveal far more than the raw inputs.
Multi-agent systems and data leakage between agents Agentic AI is increasingly multi-agent. A user-facing assistant delegates tasks to specialised sub-agents — a browsing agent, a coding agent, a scheduling agent — which may be operated by different providers, running on different infrastructure, subject to different privacy policies.
Each handoff between agents is a potential data leakage point. When the orchestrating agent sends context to a sub-agent, it may include information that is irrelevant to the sub-task but that was present in the conversation history. The sub-agent’s provider now has access to that information. Whether they store it, use it to improve their models, or share it with third parties depends on their own policies — which the end user almost certainly has not read.
This is not a hypothetical. The MCP protocol, which standardises how agents expose tools to other agents, makes it straightforward to build these multi-agent pipelines. It also makes the data provenance of a complex agent workflow essentially invisible to the end user.
Consent and the delegation problem When you authorise an AI agent to act on your behalf, you are, in some sense, consenting to whatever that agent does. But this consent has limits that current frameworks are not equipped to handle.
You consent to the agent booking a flight. Does that consent extend to the agent reading your email to find your passport number? To storing your passport number for future use? To the agent’s provider using that interaction to train its next model?
The concept of meaningful consent — consent that is informed, specific, and freely given — becomes difficult to operationalise when the action space of the system is effectively unbounded. GDPR was written assuming that humans make decisions about data. When those decisions are delegated to an autonomous system, the legal categories start to strain.
What responsible design looks like I am not arguing that agentic AI is incompatible with privacy. I am arguing that building private agentic systems requires deliberate design choices that many current systems are not making.
A few things I think matter:
Minimal context passing. Agents should send only the information a sub-agent needs for its specific task. This requires explicit context management, not the default approach of passing the full conversation history.
Ephemeral memory by default. Agent memory systems should have explicit retention policies. Information that is not needed after a task completes should not persist. This is harder than it sounds, because the value of agent memory often comes from retaining context across tasks — but “across tasks” should not mean “indefinitely.”
Transparent data flows. Users should be able to inspect what data their agents have accumulated and which third-party services have received it. This is a user interface problem as much as a technical one.
Adversarial robustness. Prompt injection — where malicious content in the environment …
summary: Language model agents can now browse the web, write code, book flights, and manage your calendar. They also create a new category of privacy risk that existing frameworks were not designed to handle. Here is what concerns me.
title: Agentic AI and the privacy problems we have not solved yet

summary: Quantum Federated Learning (QFL) enables distributed training of quantum machine learning models by sharing model gradients instead of raw data, but these gradients may still leak sensitive information. To address this, homomorphic encryption has been proposed as a privacy-enhancing technique. In this work, we evaluate the overhead introduced by Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) in QFL settings and assess its feasibility for real-world use. We implement multiple quantum machine learning models, including a quantum convolutional neural network (QCNN), trained in a federated setup with CKKS-encrypted parameters. Our experiments show that memory and communication overhead remain substantial, making practical deployment challenging. Reducing model size alleviates overhead but leads to decreased predictive performance, highlighting a trade-off between privacy and model complexity.
title: Understanding the Resource Cost of Fully Homomorphic Encryption in Quantum Federated Learning

content:
When I started my PhD in late 2021, I was enthusiastic about privacy-preserving machine learning in the way that most new researchers are enthusiastic about their chosen field: I thought the hard problems were mostly technical, and I thought solving them would mostly solve the underlying issue.
Four years and a thesis later, I am still enthusiastic — but differently so. The techniques are genuinely powerful. They also fail in ways that are easy to miss if you are not careful, and the field has a tendency to understate this in its marketing materials.
Here is what I actually think about the main tools in the PPML toolbox.
Federated learning is good at one specific thing Federated learning (FL) was designed to address a straightforward problem: you want to train a model on data held by multiple parties, but you cannot move the data to a central location. The solution is to move the model instead — each party trains locally, sends parameter updates to a server, the server aggregates them, and the process repeats.
This is genuinely useful. In our work on federated learning for transcriptomic data, we showed that you can train competitive models on gene expression data distributed across hospitals without ever pooling patient records. The model quality was close to the centralised baseline, and the privacy profile was meaningfully better.
What FL does not do, by itself, is provide formal privacy guarantees. Gradient updates can leak information about training data — sometimes a surprising amount of it. Membership inference attacks can determine whether a specific individual was in the training set. Gradient inversion attacks can, in some settings, reconstruct training samples from model updates alone. FL reduces the attack surface; it does not eliminate it.
Homomorphic encryption: correct but expensive Homomorphic encryption (HE) is the technique I find most intellectually satisfying and most practically frustrating. The idea — that you can perform arbitrary computations on encrypted data without ever decrypting it — sounds like it should not be possible, and for a long time it was not. The theoretical breakthrough came in 2009; practical, somewhat-efficient schemes followed over the next decade.
We used the CKKS scheme in several of our projects, including the quantum federated learning work published earlier this year. CKKS allows approximate arithmetic on encrypted real-valued data, which makes it well suited to the kinds of linear algebra operations that machine learning involves.
The catch is computational cost. In our experiments, HE operations were two to three orders of magnitude slower than their unencrypted equivalents. For a simple logistic regression, this is manageable. For a deep neural network on high-dimensional data, it becomes prohibitive. There is active research on making HE faster — better algorithms, hardware acceleration, compiler optimisations — and the numbers improve year over year. But “eventually this will be fast enough” is not the same as “this is fast enough now.”
The other issue is that HE protects data from the server during computation, but it does not protect the outputs. If you train a model using HE and then publish the model weights, those weights may still leak training data. Privacy-preserving computation and privacy-preserving outputs are different problems.
Differential privacy: rigorous but painful Differential privacy (DP) is the only technique in this list that comes with a formal mathematical guarantee: the output of a DP mechanism does not change much whether any single individual’s data is included or not, by a controlled amount ε. This is a strong statement, and it means something precise.
The problem is that making a mechanism DP requires adding noise, and the amount of noise required for meaningful privacy protection is often large enough to destroy the usefulness of the output. In our work on differentially private multi-label learning, we found that DP is significantly harder to apply in multi-label settings than the standard single-label case: the sensitivity of the gradient grows with the number of labels, which means you need more noise, which means more accuracy loss.
Choosing the right ε is also a governance problem dressed up as a technical one. What does ε = 1 actually mean for a person whose data is in the training set? The formal guarantee is rigorous; the intuitive meaning is opaque. Regulators and ethicists are still working out how DP interacts with legal frameworks like GDPR.
What I would tell a colleague starting out None of this is a reason not to use these techniques. They are the best tools we have for a genuine problem, and using them is better than not using them.
But I would encourage a new researcher to be honest about the threat model they are addressing. FL protects against a specific adversary. HE is slow. DP costs accuracy. Combining them can help — we showed this in several papers — but the combination is not magic.
The hardest part, …
summary: Federated learning, homomorphic encryption, differential privacy — the toolbox of privacy-preserving ML is impressive. But after years of working with these techniques, I have become more cautious about what they actually guarantee.
title: The honest limits of privacy-preserving machine learning

summary: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) standardizes interactions between AI agents and tools, enabling interoperability and accelerating the adoption of agentic AI systems. This creates a unique opportunity to embed trustworthiness directly at the protocol level. As an interface between agents and tools, MCP serves as a natural enforcement point, where improvements can propagate across entire ecosystems. Analyzing MCP through the European Commission’s Ethics Guidelines for Trustworthy AI, we identify fundamental shifts in how trustworthiness manifests in agentic systems, the challenges these shifts introduce, and key intervention points. We argue that MCP’s architecture provides a strong foundation for trustworthy AI and propose practical enhancements to strengthen it, enabling more responsible and reliable deployments.
title: Position: Trustworthy Model Context Protocol Enables Responsible Agentic AI

content:
Genomic and transcriptomic data are arguably the most sensitive data that exist about a person, and they are sensitive in a way that most other personal data is not. A leaked password can be changed. A leaked genome cannot. It does not just describe you, it describes your relatives, whether they consented or not, and it can be used to infer ethnicity, predisposition to disease, and traits you may not even know about yourself. Transcriptomic data, which captures which genes are actively being expressed in a cell rather than the fixed genetic code itself, carries a related kind of exposure, revealing the current state of your biology rather than a fixed blueprint of it.
At the same time, this is exactly the kind of data that medical research needs in large quantities to be useful. Precision medicine, the idea of tailoring treatment to a patient’s own biomarkers and molecular profile, only works if models are trained on data from many patients across many institutions. Traditionally, that meant centralising raw genomic data in one place, a hospital network, a biobank, or a research consortium, and hoping the centre held. I find this arrangement uncomfortable, not because the researchers involved are untrustworthy, but because it puts irreversible, deeply personal information at the mercy of a single point of failure. This tension, between the scientific value of pooling data and the risk of concentrating it, is what privacy-preserving machine learning tries to resolve, and it is a problem I have spent much of my career working on.
Keeping the data where it is: federated learning The most direct answer to “stop centralising the data” is federated learning. Instead of sending raw data anywhere, each hospital or research site trains a model locally, on its own data, and shares only the resulting model updates with a coordinating server, which combines everyone’s updates into a shared model. The raw genomes or transcriptomes never leave the building they were collected in.
The appeal is obvious: it directly addresses the biggest source of risk, a large centralised store of raw genetic data, without asking institutions to give up on collaborative research. In my own work applying this to real transcriptomic data, the model quality on offer was genuinely encouraging: federating the training did not meaningfully hold the models back compared to training on pooled data, at least when a reasonable number of institutions took part.
The pitfall is more subtle than “does it work.” Federated learning protects against a specific threat: a coordinating server that follows the rules but would look at raw data if it could. It does not protect against a server that secretly deviates from the protocol, or against a determined adversary trying to reconstruct individual records from the aggregated updates it receives. And it has diminishing returns of its own: spread the same total amount of data across too many participating sites, and each institution ends up training on such a thin slice of the problem that the shared model quietly loses the very benefit of scale that motivated pooling data in the first place. Federated learning is a genuine improvement, not a complete solution.
Adding a mathematical guarantee: differential privacy Because federated learning alone does not stop someone from working backward from the aggregated updates to individual records, it is often paired with differential privacy: adding carefully calibrated random noise to what each site shares, so that no single participant’s data can be confidently reconstructed from the result. This gives you something federated learning alone does not, a formal, mathematical guarantee about how much any one person’s data could have influenced the outcome.
The pitfall here surprised me the most in practice. I expected the trade-off between privacy and model quality to be gradual: a little more noise, a little less accuracy, a smooth curve you could tune to taste. It is not. Model quality tends to hold up reasonably well until the noise crosses a threshold needed for meaningful protection, and then it does not degrade, it collapses, becoming close to useless almost immediately after. There is very little room to negotiate between “private enough to matter” and “still a working model.” That means differential privacy cannot be treated as a dial you turn up until it feels responsible. You have to know, for your specific model and data, where the cliff actually is before deciding whether privacy and usefulness can coexist at all.
Hiding the computation itself: homomorphic encryption A structurally different answer is to encrypt the data before it ever gets exchanged, using homomorphic encryption, which allows computations to be performed directly on encrypted values without ever decrypting them. Applied to something like a genome-wide association study, this means the server coordinating the analysis across hospitals never sees anything but ciphertext, and can still …
summary: Your genome is arguably the most sensitive data that exists about you. So why do we keep asking people to hand it over to centralised databases? A look at why genomic data needs a different kind of protection, and what the alternatives actually offer.
title: Your DNA should not have to leave the building

Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) require large-scale data sharing across institutions, raising major privacy concerns. This work introduces PP-GWAS, a privacy-preserving framework enabling multi-site GWAS without exposing sensitive genomic data. By combining cryptographic techniques and distributed computation, the method ensures data confidentiality while maintaining analytical accuracy.
title: PP-GWAS: Privacy Preserving Multi-Site Genome-wide Association Studies

summary: Medical imaging plays a central role in modern healthcare, enabling applications from disease diagnosis to personalized treatment. Machine learning methods, particularly kernel methods, are widely used in this domain but face challenges due to data privacy constraints and the high dimensionality of medical images. Data is often distributed across institutions and cannot be centralized. Existing privacy-preserving approaches typically involve trade-offs between accuracy and efficiency. In this work, we introduce OKRA (Orthonormal K-fRAmes), a novel randomized encoding-based approach for efficient and privacy-preserving kernel learning on distributed medical image data. The method improves scalability while maintaining strong predictive performance.
title: Private, Efficient and Scalable Kernel Learning for Medical Image Analysis

summary: Machine learning is key in modern data analysis, but privacy concerns often limit its application to sensitive data. One widely used technique to ensure privacy is the Private Aggregation of Teacher Ensembles (PATE) framework, which trains an ensemble of teacher models on private data and transfers knowledge to a student model with formal differential privacy guarantees. While PATE has mainly been applied to binary and multi-class classification, many real-world scenarios—especially in medicine—require multi-label predictions. In such settings, a data point may be associated with multiple relevant labels rather than a single class. This paper explores the challenges of applying differentially private learning, and specifically PATE, to multi-label classification tasks, highlighting the increased complexity and trade-offs between privacy and utility.
title: Differentially Private Multi-Label Learning Is Harder Than You'd Think

summary: Machine learning on large-scale genomic or transcriptomic data is crucial for modern health applications such as precision medicine, where treatments are tailored to individual patients based on biomarkers and molecular data. However, such data is sensitive, distributed, and difficult to centralize due to privacy and regulatory constraints. Federated learning offers a solution by enabling decentralized model training without sharing raw data. In this work, we evaluate federated learning approaches on transcriptomic datasets, comparing frameworks such as TensorFlow Federated and Flower. We conduct experiments on disease prognosis and cell type classification tasks, analyzing model performance, communication costs, and system trade-offs.
title: Federated Learning on Transcriptomic Data: Model Quality and Performance Trade-offs

summary: It is challenging to implement kernel methods when data sources are distributed and cannot be joined at a trusted third party for privacy reasons. This challenge becomes even more significant when privacy-preserving approaches that introduce noise or high computational overhead are not acceptable, such as in clinical applications. To address this, we propose FLAKE, a framework for learning with anonymized kernels on horizontally distributed data. Our approach enables exact and efficient privacy-preserving computation of kernel methods by allowing data sources to mask their data while still enabling the computation of a Gram matrix. This matrix can be used to train kernel-based machine learning models such as support vector machines without compromising privacy or utility. We show that the framework prevents adversaries from reconstructing the original input data.
title: A Privacy-Preserving Framework for Collaborative Machine Learning with Kernel Methods

summary: Smart mobility is a promising approach to meet urban transport needs in an environmentally and user-friendly way. Smart mobility computes itineraries with multiple means of transportation, e.g., trams, rental bikes or electric scooters, according to customer preferences. A mobility platform cares for reservations, connecting transports, invoicing and billing. This requires sharing sensible personal data with multiple parties, and puts data privacy at risk. In this paper, we investigate if fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) can be applied in practice to mitigate such privacy issues. FHE allows to calculate on encrypted data, without having to decrypt it first. We implemented three typical distributed computations in a smart mobility scenario with SEAL, a recent programming library for FHE. With this implementation, we have measured memory consumption and execution times for three variants of distributed transactions.
title: Is Homomorphic Encryption Feasible for Smart Mobility?
